sets.title: Ethics 1
sets.desc: 2 vignettes + 15 stand-alone questions from the key notes

vignettes.body:
Alden Weston is a Level II CFA candidate. In addition to studying the curriculum independently, he and several of his coworkers have formed a study group that uses many of the resources provided by CFA Institute to prepare for the exam. They meet every Monday to review the previous week’s study materials and discuss items needing further clarification. This week’s reading is the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct. After studying the Standards, Weston answers the topic questions offered by CFA Institute. He notes three scenarios he wants to clarify with the group.

Weston brings up the first scenario and lays out the following facts given: A research analyst makes a presentation to a small group of investors. Prior to the start of the meeting, the analyst chatted with several individuals outside the meeting room. The analyst commented that she had just gotten off the phone with the CFO of a company she follows where they talked about a recently announced merger by a competitor. The analyst starts the presentation and discusses her research process and her published investment recommendations on the companies under her coverage. She mentions her call with the CFO as well as the comments she made during an interview on a major television network relating to the merger.

In the second scenario, Weston states, “I'm really struggling to understand the following two recommendations and question if they apply to Standard I(B): Independence and Objectivity:

Recommendation 1: Firms should require prior approval for employees participating in initial public offerings.

Recommendation 2: Firms should implement effective supervisory and review procedures to ensure compliance with personal investment policies.”

The final scenario he wants to discuss with the group has to do with policy recommendations made by a firm’s chief compliance officer regarding communication with clients and prospective clients. The officer provided her firm’s board the following policies for approval:

Policy 1: When discussing earnings estimates, caution should be exercised to avoid overconfidence regarding the accuracy of the earnings model.

Policy 2: If a capsule or condensed form of a recommendation is utilized in social media communications, reasonable efforts should be made to notify all clients about the social media post.

Policy 3: Significant changes in risk characteristics for either a security or asset strategy should be communicated to all clients.

During their gathering, Weston and his coworkers also discuss how they could unintentionally violate Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate. The group affirms their commitment to the high ethical standards of CFA Institute and talks about how a violation might occur. They make the following pledges to help each other stay in compliance with Standard VII following the exam:

Pledge 1: Abstain from making any comments about the curriculum on social media.

Pledge 2: Refrain from expressing negative comments about the CFA Program.

Pledge 3: Avoid discussing the particulars of the topic areas tested with each other.

questions.q: In the first scenario Weston discusses, did the research analyst most likely violate any CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Yes, with regard to the presentation.
Yes, with regard to the discussion prior to the presentation.
No.
questions.why: In the first scenario Weston provides no evidence of any violation of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct. The discussion prior to the meeting is not a violation of Standard II(A): Material Nonpublic Information. Standard II(A) states Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information.

questions.q: Do the recommendations Weston outlines in the second scenario most likely apply to Standard I(B): Independence and Objectivity?
options: Yes.
No, with regard to Recommendation 2.
No, with regard to Recommendation 1.
questions.why: Both Recommendation 1 (“Firms should require prior approval for employees participating in initial public offerings.”) and Recommendation 2 (“Firms should implement effective supervisory and review procedures to ensure compliance with personal investment policies.”) apply to Standard I(B): Independence and Objectivity.

questions.q: In the third scenario, which policy presented by the chief compliance officer would least likely be fully compliant with Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions?
options: Policy 3
Policy 1
Policy 2
questions.why: Policy 2 (“If a capsule or condensed form of a recommendation is utilized in social media communications, reasonable efforts should be made to notify all clients about the social medial post.”) is not fully compliant with Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions. When using social media, every effort should be made to treat clients fairly.

questions.q: Which of the study group’s pledges would most likely be required to ensure compliance with Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate?
options: Pledge 3
Pledge 2
Pledge 1
questions.why: Pledge 3 (Avoid discussing the particulars of the topic areas tested with each other.) would be required to ensure compliance with Standard VII: Responsibilities as a CFA Institute Member or CFA Candidate.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Margie Germainne, CFA, is a risk management consultant who has been asked by a small investment bank to recommend policies to prevent bank employees from front-running client orders. These clients generally invest in one or more of the bank’s large cap equity unit trusts. To ensure compliance with the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, Germainne should least likely recommend which of the following? Employees should be restricted from trading:
options: without prior permission.
during established time periods.
equity related securities.
questions.why: Correct because while Standard VI(B)–Priority of Transactions is designed to prevent any potential conflict of interest or the appearance of a conflict of interest with respect to personal transactions, it does not ban employees from trading securities. A ban on all equity related securities could be excessively restrictive to employees and unnecessary if appropriate personal transaction policies and procedures are in place.

questions.q: Offering your employer's research to another firm in hope of a future job and equity stake there also breaches:
options: I(B) Independence and Objectivity
III(C) Suitability and client objectives
VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute
questions.why: The hoped-for job and equity are a benefit that could compromise objectivity: I(B) forbids offering or accepting such consideration.

questions.q: Ileana Inkster, CFA, was recently offered a senior management position within the trust department at a regional bank. The department is new, but the bank has plans to expand it significantly over the next few months. Inkster has been told she will be expected to help grow the client base of the trust department. She is informed that the trust department plans to conduct educational seminars and pursue the attendees as new clients. Inkster notices that recent seminar advertisements prepared by the bank’s marketing department do not mention that investment products will be for sale at the seminar. The ads indicate attendees can “learn how to immediately add $100,000 to their net worth.” What should Inkster most likely do to avoid violating any CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Decline to accept the new position
Accept the position and revise the marketing material
Accept the position and inform senior management of inadequate compliance procedures
questions.why: Correct because the prospective supervisor’s first step should be to not take the position. Accepting the position with inadequate procedures in place or improper marketing material would leave Inkster at risk of incurring a violation of the Code and Standards—Standard IV(C)–Responsibilities of Supervisors.

questions.q: Bronson provides investment advice to the board of trustees of a private university endowment fund. The trustees have provided Bronson with the fund’s financial information, including planned expenditures. Bronson receives a phone call on Friday afternoon from Murdock, a prominent alumnus, requesting that Bronson fax him comprehensive financial information about the fund. According to Murdock, he has a potential contributor but needs the information that day to close the deal and cannot contact any of the trustees. Based on the CFA Institute Standards, Bronson should:
options: not send Murdock the information, to preserve confidentiality.
send Murdock the information, provided Bronson promptly notifies the trustees.
send Murdock the information because disclosure would benefit the client.
questions.why: This question relates to Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care and Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality. In this case, the member manages funds of a private endowment. Clients—in this case, the trustees of the fund—must place some trust in members and candidates.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Asking a current client with first-hand experience of your work for a reference letter is:
options: Allowed only after you leave the firm
Generally consistent with I(B)
A violation, since clients can't be asked
questions.why: A client who knows your work and has nothing to gain can give an objective reference, so I(B) isn't compromised.

questions.q: Which fee arrangement for issuer-paid research best supports independence?
options: Payment partly in the issuer's shares
A fee that is higher if the report is favourable
Full disclosure of the arrangement and a flat fee, with no bonus, regardless of the conclusion or recommendation
questions.why: Compensation must not depend on the conclusion (I(B), VI(A)). Disclose the arrangement and use a flat fee without bonus.

questions.q: A company is rearranging its factory layout, which raises efficiency but needs no new machinery or personnel. An analyst learns of it. The information is:
options: Probably not material nonpublic information
Material, because it affects efficiency
Nonpublic, so it cannot be used
questions.why: Information is material if it would affect the price or an investor's decision. A layout change with no new machinery or staff is unlikely to.

vignettes.body:
Marisa Cheng, CFA, is a portfolio manager with a large full-service investment advisory firm. She has been invited to speak on a podcast with a target audience of recent university graduates entering the investment industry. Cheng decided to focus her talk on her favorite topic: “How to Advance Your Career.” During the podcast, she mentions that most portfolio managers start in the Research Department. She then shares her philosophy that when entering the industry as an entry-level research analyst, you should create a research report at least once a week to prove yourself. This is particularly easy if you are an equity analyst, as the research analysis process should be the same regardless of the security being analyzed.

Cheng then offers advice to the audience about the benefits of changing employers, which she believes allows a person to move into higher positions with greater responsibilities. She explains “Based on my experience, younger employees get overlooked when employers are filling middle to senior management positions. By moving to a different firm every three to five years, you can typically join at a more senior level with higher pay. However, when you move to a new firm, you need to be cautious so your employer and client relationships are not harmed.”

Cheng recommends the following actions:

# Action 1: | Notify clients of your new role before changing employers.
Action 2: | Utilize your own viewpoints based on your skills and experiences.
Action 3: | Share policies and processes utilized in past positions.

The podcast interviewer asks, “I know this is a bit off today’s topic, but I was wondering, as a CFA® charterholder, how do you ensure you are serving your clients’ interests as required by the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct? For instance, what would you do if you learned in a meeting with your client that due to a change in their circumstances, the investment product they have invested in no longer meets their investment goals and constraints outlined in their investment policy statement?”

Cheng responds, “Let’s consider three options.”

# Option 1: | I could immediately reassure them their existing product is still suitable even under their changing circumstances.
Option 2: | I could advise them to shop around to determine whether other investment management firms had a more appropriate product to meet their investment goals and give them a list of questions to ask so they could compare services.
Option 3: | I could advise them to add some of our other investment products to their existing investment portfolio, so their new overall investment return objectives and risk profile could be met given their new circumstances.

After thanking the interviewer for the opportunity to speak, Cheng makes the following final statement:

“I would like to encourage all the listeners who are interested in advancing their careers in the investment industry to become CFA charterholders. The three sequential exams are very tough, as you can be tested on a wide array of curriculum topics, including financial analysis, economics, and derivatives. Becoming a charterholder also demonstrates you are more professional than those without the CFA® charter. By upholding the CFA Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct, you send a message to the industry that you really care about the interests of your clients and the integrity of the capital markets.”

questions.q: Is Cheng’s philosophy regarding an entry-level research analyst role most likely consistent with guidance for Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis?
options: Yes, with regard to the equity analysis process.
No.
Yes, with regard to weekly research reports.
questions.why: Cheng’s philosophy regarding an entry-level research analyst’s role – that is, you should create a research report at least once a week and it is particularly easy if you are an equity analyst as the research process is the same regardless of the security – is inconsistent with the guidance for Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis.

questions.q: Given Cheng’s advice regarding changing jobs, which recommended action should an employee most likely take to avoid violating the CFA Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Action 1
Action 2
Action 3
questions.why: A member or candidate is allowed to utilize their viewpoints based on their skills and the experiences gained from their former employment without violating Standard IV(A) Loyalty. By doing so, they would not potentially harm their former employer.

questions.q: To avoid violating CFA Standards of Professional Conduct, which of Cheng’s options in response to the interviewer’s question is least appropriate?
options: Option 1
Option 3
Option 2
questions.why: Option 1, I could immediately reassure them their existing product is still suitable even under their changing circumstances, would not be appropriate. Before giving any investment advice, Cheng should better understand the changing circumstances of the client and determine whether the existing product is still suitable rather than immediately state that it is.

questions.q: Which component of Cheng’s final statement most likely causes her to violate CFA Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Comment on testing and curriculum
The message to the industry
A CFA charterholder’s level of professionalism
questions.why: Cheng’s comment, “Becoming a charterholder also demonstrates you are more professional than those without the CFA charter, violates Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA® designation, and the CFA® Program. By making such a claim, she is exaggerating the meaning of the charter.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: A firm claims to comply with GIPS when it does not. This violates:
options: Nothing, because GIPS compliance is voluntary
III(D) Performance Presentation
Only V(B) Communication with Clients
questions.why: Claiming GIPS compliance when not compliant is a misrepresentation in performance presentation.

questions.q: Under III(B) Fair Dealing, when a recommendation changes, the firm should notify:
options: All clients, especially those who acted on it
Only clients who still hold the security
Only clients who later ask about the change
questions.why: Changed recommendations should go to all clients, with priority to those who acted on the earlier advice.

questions.q: A member suspects illegal activity by a client. Disclosing it to the authorities is:
options: Prohibited, because client information is confidential
Permitted only if the client is a key client of the firm
Permitted as an exception to confidentiality, whether the client is ordinary or a key client
questions.why: III(E) exceptions include illegal activity. The size or importance of the client does not matter.

questions.q: If an employee's outside paid arrangement could affect clients, the firm should also:
options: Ask the CFA Institute to approve it first
Only keep the signed contract on file
Disclose it to clients and prospects (VI(A))
questions.why: VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts: matters that could impair independence or interfere with duties to clients must be fully and fairly disclosed.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Richard Cardinal, CFA, is the founder of Volcano Capital Research, an investment management firm whose sole activity is short selling. Cardinal seeks out companies whose stocks have had large price increases. Cardinal also pays several lobbying firms to update him immediately on any legislative or regulatory changes that may impact his target companies. Cardinal sells short those target companies he estimates are near the peak of their sales and earnings and that his sources identify as facing legal or regulatory challenges. Immediately after he sells a stock, Cardinal conducts a public relations campaign to disclose all of the negative information he has gathered on the company, even if the information is not yet public. Which of Cardinal’s following actions is most likely to be in violation of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Selling stock short
Trading on information from lobbyists
Disclosing information about target companies
questions.why: Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because selling stock short is a management strategy and does not necessarily violate any aspect of the Code and Standards. Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it appears a reasonable and diligent effort has been made as required by Standard V(A)–Diligence and Reasonable Basis to determine the investment action is sound and suitable for his clients.

questions.q: A client says their broker does not give best execution, yet tells the analyst to keep using that broker, and the analyst does. This is:
options: Not a violation: the client directs the brokerage
A violation of VI(A) Disclosure of Conflicts
A violation of III(A) because best execution is required
questions.why: When the client directs the broker, the member is following the client's instruction, so there is no violation.

questions.q: Offering introductions to influential people to win a consulting assignment most likely violates:
options: Standard I(C), Misrepresentation
Standard VI(A), Disclosure of Conflicts
Standard I(B), Independence and Objectivity
questions.why: Offering benefits that could reasonably compromise someone's independence in choosing an adviser breaches I(B).

questions.q: A member under investigation by CFA Institute's Professional Conduct Program (PCP) faces possible sanctions. Must the member tell clients about the possible sanctions?
options: Yes, immediately, under VI(A)
No: the sanctions are not yet official
Yes, but only the key clients
questions.why: Possible sanctions are not officialised until the process ends, so there is nothing to disclose yet.

sets.title: Ethics 2
sets.desc: 2 vignettes + 15 stand-alone questions from the key notes

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Written due-diligence procedures for judging whether a recommendation has adequate support relate to:
options: Reasonable Basis
Compensation
Distribution
questions.why: V(A) recommended procedures: Reasonable Basis = written due-diligence standards; Distribution = supervisory approval; Compensation = measurable quality criteria.

questions.q: Jeffrey Jones passed the Level I CFA exam in 1997 and the Level II exam in 2009. He is not currently enrolled for the Level III exam. According to the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, which of the following is the most appropriate way for Jones to refer to his participation in the CFA Program?
options: Jeffrey Jones, CFA (expected 2014)
Candidate in the CFA Institute CFA Program
Passed Level II of the CFA examination in 2009
questions.why: Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because it is an improper reference to use “expected” as part of the designation. Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because a person can only state he is a Candidate if he is currently enrolled in the CFA Program. Correct Answer Feedback: Correct because no designation exists for someone who has passed Level I, Level II, or Level III of the CFA exam [Standard VII(B)].

questions.q: Having a supervisory analyst approve research before it is sent to clients is the V(A) procedure for:
options: Reasonable basis
Compensation
Distribution
questions.why: Distribution: review and approval before external circulation, to check the firm's criteria are met.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: A gift that creates no conflict and does not compete with the employer's interests is:
options: A violation of I(B) in all cases
Acceptable only after a written ruling from the CFA Institute
Fine
questions.why: The standards target gifts that could compromise objectivity or conflict with the employer. Other gifts are fine.

questions.q: While employed by A and planning to move to B, a worker uses a personal laptop after hours to list what they did for A. This is:
options: A violation unless A consents in writing
Not a violation, as long as the list contains no confidential employer information
A violation of IV(A) because the work belongs to A
questions.why: A record of one's own work history is not confidential information, and it is made outside working hours.

questions.q: The mosaic theory holds that an analyst:
options: can use material public information and nonmaterial nonpublic information in the analyst’s analysis.
violates the Code and Standards if the analyst fails to have knowledge of and comply with applicable laws.
should use all available and relevant information in support of an investment recommendation.
questions.why: This question deals with Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information. The mosaic theory states that an analyst may use material public information and nonmaterial nonpublic information in creating a larger picture than shown by any individual piece of information and the conclusions the analyst reaches become material only after the pieces are assembled.

questions.q: Under IV(A), members who leave a firm may take records, files or models only with:
options: The employer's written permission, even if the person who developed the model agrees
No permission, if they built the model themselves
The written consent of the person who developed the model
questions.why: Records and models created at work belong to the employer. The developer's own consent is not enough.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Under III(B), all accounts in the same block trade should receive:
options: The same price and commission
Prices that reflect each account's size
The price in the order they were entered
questions.why: Fair allocation: every account in a block trade gets the same execution price and is charged the same commission.

questions.q: Client information is confidential for:
options: Current clients only
Former, current and prospective clients
Current and prospective clients, not former ones
questions.why: III(E) covers all client information, whatever the status of the relationship.

questions.q: A firm caps gifts at USD100 each. A CFO sends six USD100 baskets, shared one per team member. This is:
options: Acceptable only if reported to clients
A breach of firm policy and I(D)
Consistent with policy: no violation
questions.why: Each person receives one gift within the limit, so firm policy is followed and objectivity is unlikely to be compromised.

questions.q: Standard II(B) Market Manipulation covers:
options: Only spreading false information
Only trades that create false prices
Both information- and transaction-based
questions.why: II(B) covers distorting prices with misleading information AND trades that create false liquidity or price levels.

vignettes.body:
Suzy Mercer, CFA, is currently working as a capital market adviser in a developing country. While attending a regional securities exchange conference, she introduces herself to Terrence Ong, CFA. Ong is one of several partners at Shangri-la Development Associates, a consulting firm specializing in capital market expansion in developing countries. When making her introduction, Mercer states, “I’m an independent adviser working with the government of a developing country to improve its capital market sector. I’ve heard a lot about the work you’ve done. Could we talk about my consulting assignment and a possible role for you?”

Mercer continues, “I’m looking for someone with your background and stellar reputation to help create a strategic plan to develop the asset management industry. The client’s goal is to get the Securities Exchange to be a part of a regional exchange. This will help the locally listed companies gain more exposure. However, given the budget I’ve been given, I can afford to hire only an individual. Ong, would this be of interest to you?”

Mercer continues the conversation by informing Ong that she will also be approaching other industry participants, particularly in the fund management industry, who are attending the conference. Ong responds, “I sure hope you are not talking to Daniel Ngyue, who manages several startup funds. I think he has a drinking problem. There is a rumor his last startup fund was not well received by the investors, likely due to his drinking. As one charterholder to another, please do your due diligence first before you hire anyone. As you have already pointed out, my reputation is stellar. Why don’t we meet tonight for dinner at my ‘members only’ club to discuss your project further? I can introduce you to other influential people who are currently looking for experienced advisers in your field for upcoming assignments. I’m sure if they knew we were working together, it would really go a long way in obtaining future assignments from these industry leaders.”

Mercer informs Ong that she is unfortunately not able to meet him for dinner because of a previous engagement. She subsequently says to Ong, “I’m wondering how you would respond to a situation whereby a regulator chooses not to implement extensive policies and regulations regarding the integrity of capital markets I recommended. They say my suggested policies and regulations related to market manipulation, material nonpublic information, and protecting client interests are too complicated, and they do not have the judicial competency to back them up. Consequently, they have requested I recommend just one primary rule.” Thereafter, Mercer seeks out Daniel Ngyue, a CFA candidate, to ask for his version of what happened with his investors. Ngyue responds, “What actually happened was I got sick in a restaurant after having an adverse reaction to some medication. People uploaded photos to social media and stated I was falling over drunk. Subsequently, I wrote a letter to the investors explaining the situation and assuring them I had found another highly qualified fund manager after several weeks to take over until such time I had fully recovered. When I could, I looked at the fund when I was in the hospital for a week, but the fund needs close supervision, so that’s why I wanted to find another manager. One investor commented, ‘Key-person risk was not identified in the fund’s prospectus.’ Within one week we sent out a revision to the prospectus identifying key-person risk.”

questions.q: To avoid violating any CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, which of the following is Ong’s most appropriate response to Mercer’s question?
options: “I will need to touch base with my partners.”
“I can refer you to another independent adviser.”
“I’m not able to take on projects as an individual.”
questions.why: Ong’s most appropriate response is, “I will need to touch base with my Partners.” Ong has a responsibility to protect the interests of his firm and his partners, according to Standard IV: Duty to Employers. If Ong took the assignment as an individual, he would be potentially harming his firm and his fellow partners.

questions.q: In the continued conversation between Mercer and Ong, which sub-standard of Standard I: Professionalism did Ong least likely violate?
options: Independence and Objectivity
Misrepresentation
Misconduct
questions.why: Correct, because Ong least likely violated Standard I(C): Misrepresentation when stating he had a stellar reputation, since Mercer had previously noted it as one of the reasons why she was talking to him, so it is unlikely he misrepresented himself. Ong, however, did violate Standard I(A): Misconduct by maligning the reputation of Daniel Ngyue on the basis of his speculation about Ngyue’s drinking and a rumor he heard.

questions.q: Which of the following should Ong most likely advise with regard to the regulator’s request?
options: Require material information be made public within 24 hours
When trading, insist service providers give preference to investors
Ban the “pumping up” of investment prices
questions.why: Ong should insist service providers give preference to investors when trading. By assuring investor interests are given preference or priority, the regulators would be helping to maintain capital market integrity. This would also comply with Standard IV(A): Loyalty, Prudence, and Care.

questions.q: During the conversation between Ngyue and Mercer, Ngyue revealed he had most likely violated which CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Standard I: Professionalism
Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions
Both Standard I: Professionalism and Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions
questions.why: It is apparent Ngyue revealed he had violated both Standard I: Professionalism and Standard V: Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions. Specifically, he likely violated Standard I(C): Misrepresentation by making an omission when key-person risk was absent from the fund prospectus.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Buying a stock for every client in one block trade, favouring no one, satisfies Fair Dealing but may still breach:
options: III(C) Suitability
II(B) Market Manipulation
VI(B) Priority of Transactions
questions.why: Treating everyone the same is fair, but the stock must still fit each account's objectives and constraints.

questions.q: A 2012 'buy' recommendation relies on 2008–2010 data and a CAGR. This most likely violates:
options: V(B) Communication with Clients: it relies on dated information
VI(C) Referral Fees
III(B) Fair Dealing
questions.why: Recommendations must rest on current information. Citing old data without making that clear misleads clients.

questions.q:
Grey recommends the purchase of a mutual fund that invests solely in long-term US Treasury bonds. He makes the following statements to his clients: 

I. “The payment of the bonds is guaranteed by the US government; therefore, the default risk of the bonds is virtually zero.” 

II. “If you invest in the mutual fund, you will earn a 10% rate of return each year for the next several years based on historical performance of the market.” 

Did Grey’s statements violate the CFA Institute Code and Standards?
options: Neither statement violated the Code and Standards.
Only statement II violated the Code and Standards.
Only statement I violated the Code and Standards.
questions.why: This question involves Standard I(C) Misrepresentation. Statement I is a factual statement that discloses to clients and prospects accurate information about the terms of the investment instrument. Statement II, which guarantees a specific rate of return for a mutual fund, is an opinion stated as a fact and, therefore, violates Standard I(C).

questions.q: Hinting you will recommend a research provider to your next employer in return for a reference most likely violates:
options: IV(B) Additional Compensation
I(B) Independence and Objectivity
III(B) Fair Dealing among all clients
questions.why: The promised business is a benefit that could compromise your future independence in choosing research providers: I(B).

vignettes.body:
After spending years employed as a research analyst covering Asian exchanges at an investment management firm based in Singapore and then undertaking further training, Vishram Mehta, CFA, recently launched a new career as an independent asset consultant. His first client is Montfill Tech (“Montfill”), a small software development company with offices in Singapore and India. Montfill is struggling to retain top developers for more than two years. Consequently, the company feels it is not able to fully capitalize on the investments it has made in employee training and development. Montfill is considering introducing a retirement benefit plan to supplement the statutory government-sponsored individual employee defined contribution (DC) plans. It feels the extra benefit designed with no risk to the employee will help with retention. Mehta’s assignment is to design a defined benefit (DB) package that includes an Investment Policy Statement and asset allocation.

To begin the assignment, Mehta researches the rules and regulations concerning pension plans in Singapore and India. Mehta initially thinks the pension plan regulations are tougher in India than in Singapore. Given the extensive regulations, however, he realizes he needs some help and thus considers speaking with an expert in global pension plan regulations. Subsequently, during a short conversation with a manager working in the Human Resources (HR) department of a multinational, Mehta asks the manager to outline the prominent features of their pension plan. Mehta contemplates what his next step should be based on the information he has received so far.

To start determining an asset allocation for Montfill’s DB plan, Mehta reviews the answers he captured during his initial conversations with management to help him assess Montfill’s investment profile, including return objectives, risk tolerances, previous investment history, and current and projected financial status. He has yet to receive the detailed answers to the questionnaire he sent to Montfill’s HR department about employee demographics. While he is awaiting the questionnaire responses, he drafts an asset allocation based on his understanding of the client’s needs.

Before Mehta begins to draft the Investment Policy Statement, he recalls the earlier conversation he had with the HR manager. The HR manager advised him to have a consultation with Risner Employee Benefits Law, a global legal firm with a stellar reputation in over 150 countries. The HR manager also mentioned Mehta might want to offer his services as a pension trustee or consultant to the client given all his years of experience in Asia. Mehta remembers his remarks: “Those are great ideas, particularly as I have direct work experience in all the countries where my client operates. I think I might also recommend that Risner draft the needed legal documents if I find their services are appropriate after my conversation and due diligence. But I’ll work out a referral fee arrangement first and include those details in my recommendation to the client.”

Mehta wants to include the following items in the Investment Policy Statement:

As previously disclosed in the contract between us:

Item 1: In lieu of evaluating new providers of third-party economic research needed to help determine asset class return forecasts, I hired those used by my former employer. The fees I pay them are part of normal operating expenses so are not directly expensed back to the client.

Item 2: As an independent asset consultant, there may be times when I am working on similar projects concurrently. These assignments may be for clients within the same industry (i.e., competitors). Systems and processes are in place to protect the privacy and data of all clients.

Item 3: Each assignment is undertaken with the best interests of the client in mind to meet their overall objectives as defined in our contract. It is up to each client to seek outside legal counsel and implement only the recommendations they deem fit.

questions.q: What should Mehta’s next step most likely be to avoid violating the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Consult with a legal specialist.
Replicate the multinational firm’s pension plan.
Limit his research to India.
questions.why: To avoid violating Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law, Mehta should consult with legal specialists who understand the pension regulations in both Singapore and India. He has recognized he needs help after his initial desktop research. If he limited his desktop research to India, he would likely be violating Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law in that he would not take into consideration Singaporean regulations.

questions.q: Will Mehta’s draft asset allocation recommendation most likely conform to Standard III(C): Suitability?
options: No, with regard to Montfill’s profile
No, with regard to the HR department request
Yes
questions.why: Mehta’s draft asset allocation will most likely violate Standard III(C) given he has not received responses to the questionnaire addressing employee demographics. To understand liquidity needs of the funds, it is critical to understand the age profile of the client’s labor force, any planned early retirements due to known medical conditions, etc.

questions.q: If Mehta proposes Risner’s and his services to his client (Montfill), which component of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct will least likely be violated?
options: Misconduct
Misrepresentation
Referral fees
questions.why: Mehta would least likely violate Standard VI(C): Referral Fees as he noted he will include any referral fee arrangements in the proposal to Montfill. Standard VI(C): Referral Fees requires Members and Candidates to disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services.

questions.q: Which of the items Mehta wants to include in the Investment Policy Statement most likely reflects a violation of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Item 2
Item 1
Item 3
questions.why: Item 1 most likely reflects a violation of the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct. Mehta is using economic data from third-party providers to help determine expected asset class returns to formulate his asset class recommendations to clients.

sets.title: Ethics 3
sets.desc: 2 vignettes + 15 stand-alone questions from the key notes

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: A friend refers clients to a member. With no payment, the member says, "I'll at least pay for our holiday." The member must:
options: Disclose only to the employer
Disclose nothing: no cash fee was paid
Disclose the travel expenses to both clients and the employer
questions.why: VI(C): any compensation, consideration or benefit received or paid to others for recommending products or services must be disclosed to clients and the employer.

questions.q: Which procedures does VI(B), Priority of Transactions, recommend for personal trades?
options: Pre-clearance of trades (compliance approval) and duplicate trade confirmations or statements sent by the broker to the employer
Annual holdings reports only
No pre-clearance, but a quarterly review of all trades
questions.why: VI(B) recommends pre-clearance and having the broker send copies of personal trade confirmations or account statements to the employer.

questions.q: Which one of the following actions will help ensure the fair treatment of brokerage firm clients when a new investment recommendation is made?
options: Informing all people in the firm in advance that a recommendation is to be disseminated
Distributing recommendations to institutional clients prior to individual accounts
Minimizing the time between the decision and the dissemination of a recommendation
questions.why: This question, which relates to Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, tests the knowledge of the procedures that will assist members and candidates in treating clients fairly when making investment recommendations. Minimizing the time between the decision and the dissemination will help ensure the fair treatment of clients. Informing all people in the firm in advance may have negative effects on the fair treatment of clients.

questions.q: Which is NOT an exception to III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality?
options: The client permits the disclosure
Disclosure required by law
Disclosing a well-known client to win new business
questions.why: Exceptions: PCP claim defence, illegal activity by the client, disclosure required by law, and client permission.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: A member accepts a paid position that does not compete with the employer. Under the Standards:
options: It must be disclosed to clients under VI(A)
Written consent from the employer is always required
There is no need to disclose the position
questions.why: IV(B) concerns compensation that competes with, or creates a conflict with, the employer. A paid role that does not compete needs no disclosure.

questions.q: In a research report, an analysis that is not a critical component of the analysis or the resulting recommendation:
options: Must be kept for seven years
Must be sent to clients with the report
Does not need to be retained under V(C)
questions.why: V(C): keep records that support the key analysis and recommendation. Non-critical items need not be kept.

questions.q: Under Standard IV(C), supervisors' compliance procedures should be reviewed:
options: Only after a violation has been discovered and reported
Once, when the compliance program is first adopted
Periodically, and whenever laws or regulations change
questions.why: Supervisors must keep procedures adequate over time: periodic reviews and updates, plus revisions when new laws or regulations arrive.

vignettes.body:
Rodrick Darko, CFA, is a senior research analyst at TTN Capital, a large full-service brokerage and investment firm. Darko is invited to an analyst conference hosted by Bloom Data Centers, a company covered by Darko. Bloom arranges to pay for the commercial flights for all analysts attending the conference. Bloom also provides a company-branded mug as a gift to all analysts who attend the conference. Darko accepts the travel arrangement and the gift.

Darko is building a model to support his analysis for a research report on Ncenter Corp. As a source for the model, Darko relies on a third-party research provider that was approved by TTN's research division. He does not perform his own due diligence on the research provider. Darko's analysis includes both positive and negative growth scenarios in the model, but Darko decides to include only the positive growth scenario in his report.

Darko's supervisor is concerned about recent policy violations by employees in his department. During a compliance training meeting, Darko suggests three initiatives to improve compliance.

Initiative 1: Periodically update compliance procedures to ensure that the measures are adequate under the law

Initiative 2: Educate personnel regarding the compliance procedures only when they join the firm

Initiative 3: Issue periodic reminders of the compliance procedures to appropriate personnel

Anne Garcia, CFA, works in TTN's client services department. Garcia meets with a client and, during the meeting, she receives information that makes her suspect the client has committed tax fraud. Garcia sends a company-wide email detailing her suspicions. The regulator contacts Garcia as part of its investigation into the client's suspected tax fraud and requests that Garcia send information regarding the client to the regulator. Garcia provides the information to the regulator as required by local law.

questions.q: Does Darko violate the Standards regarding the Bloom conference?
options: Yes, by accepting the travel arrangement only
No
Yes, by accepting the travel arrangement and the gift
questions.why: Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Darko violates Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity by accepting the travel arrangement. According to the guidance for Standard I(B), to avoid the appearance of compromising their independence and objectivity, best practice dictates that Members and Candidates always use commercial transportation at their expense or at the expense of their firm rather than accept paid travel…

questions.q: Does Darko violate the Standards regarding his work on the Ncenter research report?
options: Yes, regarding the third-party research provider
No
Yes, regarding his scenario choice in the report
questions.why: Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Darko violates Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis by including only the positive growth scenario and omitting the negative growth scenario. He does not violate the Standards by using third-party research which was approved by TTN's research division.

questions.q: Which compliance initiative suggested by Darko is not consistent with the Standards?
options: Initiative 1
Initiative 2
Initiative 3
questions.why: Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because, as per the guidance under Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, once a compliance program is in place, a supervisor should periodically update procedures to ensure that the measures are adequate under the law. The suggested initiative to periodically update procedures to ensure that the measures are adequate under the law is in line with the principles of Standard IV(C).

questions.q: Do Garcia's actions regarding her client's suspected tax fraud violate the Standards?
options: Yes, by sharing the information in the email
Yes, by sharing the information with the regulator
No
questions.why: Incorrect Answer Feedback: Incorrect because Garcia violates Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality by sending information about a specific client's suspected tax fraud to all internal personnel of her company via email. The principles of Standard III(E) require that members and candidates preserve the confidentiality of information communicated to them by their clients, prospective clients, and former clients.

vignettes.body:
Fiona O’Connor, CFA, who is based in Dublin, runs the asset management firm that manages the assets for the Step Up Social Impact Private Equity Fund (the Fund), which is registered in Ireland. The general partner of the Fund has asked O’Connor to meet with Elise Jensen, CFA, a pension asset consultant, to find out whether Jensen will pitch the Fund to her institutional clients looking for an environmental, social, and governance (ESG) approach. Jensen specializes in working with continental European–based pension funds, many of which are Swiss pension funds required by Swiss pension regulations to undertake an ESG assessment prior to making an investment. In addition, all her clients have a relatively low risk profile, because they are small funds. The few pension funds Jensen works with that do not require an ESG assessment still include the desire for this type of evaluation in their investment mandate.

During an introductory meeting that lasts about an hour, Jensen asks O’Connor to give an overview of the Fund. O’Connor makes the following three statements:

First, as you are aware, the Step Up Fund is a global social impact fund. Therefore, we have allocated 85% of our investment portfolio to education and health care. In addition, some of the companies we invest in offer scholarships or free services to those who cannot afford their services. As a result, our investment returns may not be as high as those of funds that have a strict “for-profit” investment strategy, but we still track our Fund against ESG indexes. We have also developed a set of “social impact” metrics that aim to show the Fund has a positive impact on people’s lives. Details of the investment strategy and how we select investments are clearly and extensively described in our fund prospectus. In addition, investors are notified prior to any changes being made in our investment process.

Second, let me explain how we select investments. I’ll give you the prospectus, too, for your further reference, because it contains all the details, and they’re quite extensive. We identify potential investments from around the globe through our own analysts’ research within the education and health care industries. We also use third-party agents to find potential investments. If we make an investment in the companies they present to us, we pay them a finder’s fee. One such agent we use is Make-a-Difference Consultants, an asset consulting firm that has adopted the CFA Institute Code and Standards.

Finally, I also want to disclose to you the compensation arrangements for the asset management firm’s six investment analysts, all of whom report to me directly. Two of the analysts work part-time, because they made earlier commitments with other asset management firms before I found them. But they do not work for other social impact funds, so I’m OK with this arrangement because we consider them independent contractors. We disclose this and other forms of management compensation to all clients and potential clients. All the analysts are paid monthly and participate in the firm’s year-end bonus program. The value of the bonus pool is determined by how well the company has performed.

questions.q: Based only on the information given, when providing investment advice to her clients, Jensen should most likely adhere to which of the following to avoid violating Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law?
options: Swiss regulations
Irish legislation
CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct
questions.why: Jensen should adhere to Swiss regulations. Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law requires members and candidates to adhere to the stricter of any applicable legislation or regulations and the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct.

questions.q: Given O’Connor’s first statement about the asset allocation, expected returns, and strategy of the Step Up Social Impact Private Equity Fund, does O’Connor most likely violate the CFA Institute Standards?
options: Yes, with regard to Standard III(A): Loyalty, Prudence, and Care
Yes, with regard to Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients
No
questions.why: Correct because there is no indication O’Connor violated Standard III(A): Loyalty, Prudence, and Care or Standard V(B): Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients. With regard to Standard III(A), investors in this type of social impact fund are likely looking to achieve high levels of social impact as well as to obtain somewhat competitive investment returns.

questions.q: Given O’Connor’s second statement to Jensen, which further action should O’Connor least likely take to comply with required or recommended procedures for the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct?
options: Disclose the finder’s fee arrangement in the fund prospectus.
Monitor the consultants’ compliance policy execution.
Notify clients of the finder’s fee policy on a semiannual basis.
questions.why: O’Connor should least likely notify clients of the finder’s fee policy on a semiannual basis. Recommended procedures to implement Standard VI(C): Referral Fees are to notify clients at least quarterly, not semiannually.

questions.q: With regard to the asset management firm’s compensation arrangements for the investment analysts as mentioned in O’Connor’s final statement, does O’Connor most likely violate any CFA Institute Standards?
options: Yes, relating to the bonus pool
Yes, relating to the part-time policy
No
questions.why: O’Connor has not violated any CFA Institute Standards relating to the firm’s bonus pool or its part-time policy. With regard to the year-end bonus pool, Standard VI(A): Disclosure of Conflicts is not violated, because the participation in the bonus pool is not structured to provide immediate compensation or give returns based on short-term investment action with little or no long-term value creation.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Once a supervisor learns of a possible violation, IV(C) suggests:
options: Increasing supervision or restricting the person pending investigation
Reporting it to the local CFA society straight away
Waiting for the employee's next annual performance review to raise it
questions.why: Respond promptly: investigate, and increase supervision or place limits on the person while it is resolved.

questions.q: Firm A and a brokerage B agree to exchange client referrals. The arrangement complies with the Standards if it is:
options: Disclosed to clients and prospective clients
Disclosed to the employer only
Never allowed under VI(C)
questions.why: VI(C) Referral Fees: compensation or benefit for referrals must be disclosed so clients can evaluate the recommendation.

questions.q: Naming a charterholder who is under CFA Institute investigation for unethical behaviour is:
options: Acceptable, since PCP cases are always public
A violation if the case has not been announced publicly
Acceptable if the person is a colleague
questions.why: PCP matters are confidential until announced. Naming someone before that breaches confidentiality.

questions.q: Under III(B), a partially filled block order should be allocated:
options: To the largest accounts first
First-come, first-served
Pro rata across the accounts
questions.why: Pro-rata allocation of partial fills is a recommended fair-dealing procedure; it treats every participating client equally.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Analysts promoting the success or accuracy of their recommendations must:
options: Make reasonable efforts to ensure the information is fair, accurate and complete
Show only recommendations that worked
Avoid any reference to past recommendations
questions.why: III(D) Performance Presentation: promotion is allowed, but the performance information must be fair, accurate and complete.

questions.q: Requiring staff to report membership of an investment club before joining is:
options: A reasonable IV(C) preventive step
Only needed if the club trades IPOs
A breach of staff privacy
questions.why: Supervisors should have procedures that help prevent and detect violations; advance reporting does both.

questions.q: Albert and Tye, who recently started their own investment advisory business, have registered to take the Level III CFA exam. Albert’s business card reads, “Judy Albert, CFA Level II.” Tye has not put anything about the CFA designation on his business card, but promotional material that he designed for the business describes the CFA requirements and indicates that Tye participates in the CFA Program and has completed Levels I and II. According to the Standards:
options: Tye has violated the Standards, but Albert has not.
Albert has violated the Standards, but Tye has not.
both Albert and Tye have violated the Standards.
questions.why: Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program is the subject of this question. The reference on Albert’s business card implies that there is a “CFA Level II” designation; Tye merely indicates in promotional material that he is participating in the CFA Program and has completed Levels I and II.

questions.q: ABC Investment Management acquires a new, very large account with two concentrated positions. The firm’s current policy is to add new accounts for the purpose of performance calculation after the first full month of management. Cupp is responsible for calculating the firm’s performance returns. Before the end of the initial month, Cupp notices that one of the significant holdings of the new accounts is acquired by another company, causing the value of the investment to double. Because of this holding, Cupp decides to account for the new portfolio as of the date of transfer, thereby allowing ABC Investment to reap the positive impact of that month’s portfolio return. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Cupp did not violate the Code and Standards, because companies are allowed to determine when to incorporate new accounts into their composite calculation.
Cupp did not violate the Code and Standards, because the GIPS standards allow composites to be updated on the date of large external cash flows.
Cupp violated the Code and Standards because the inclusion of the new account produces an inaccurate calculation of the monthly results according to the firm’s stated policies.
questions.why: Cupp violated Standard III(D) Performance Presentations when he deviated from the firm’s stated policies solely to capture the gain from the holding being acquired. The option that GIPS allows composites to be updated on the date of large external cash flows is incorrect because the firm does not claim GIPS compliance and the GIPS standards require external cash flows to be treated in a manner consistent with the firm’s documented policies.

sets.title: Ethics 4
sets.desc: 2 vignettes + 15 stand-alone questions from the key notes

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: An analyst shares a model with a company to check facts and get comments. This is acceptable if:
options: The estimates (actual values) and the recommendation stay with the analyst and nobody gets preferential access
She gives the company the recommendation first
She adopts the company's estimates
questions.why: Fact-checking with a company is fine as long as nobody receives preferential access to the analyst's conclusions.

questions.q: Ward is scheduled to visit the corporate headquarters of Evans Industries. Ward expects to use the information he obtains there to complete his research report on Evans stock. Ward learns that Evans plans to pay all of Ward’s expenses for the trip, including the costs of meals, his hotel room, and air transportation. Which of the following actions would be the best course for Ward to take under the Code and Standards?
options: Accept the expense-paid trip, and write an objective report.
Pay for all travel expenses, including the costs of meals and incidental items.
Accept the expense-paid trip, but disclose the value of the services accepted in the report.
questions.why: The best course of action under Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is to avoid a conflict of interest whenever possible. Therefore, for Ward to pay for all his expenses is the correct answer. Accepting the trip but disclosing its value details a course of action in which the conflict would be disclosed, but the solution is not as appropriate as avoiding the conflict of interest.

questions.q:
Jenny Wilkin, CFA, leaves her employer ABC Investment (ABCI) to start her own investment firm. She has no noncompete agreement with ABCI. Wilkin leaves all research records at ABCI, and only takes an internal analysis of ABCI's sales strategy. After leaving ABCI, she uses the internet to look up the clients she served at her former firm. Using the contact data she finds on the internet, she solicits clients and encourages them to switch to her new firm.
Did Wilkin violate the Standard relating to loyalty?
options: Yes, by taking an internal analysis of ABCI's sales strategy
Yes, by soliciting business from ABCI clients to switch to her new firm
No
questions.why: Correct because according to Standard IV(A): Loyalty, the member or candidate must not take records or files to a new employer without the written permission of the previous employer. Also, firm records or work performed on behalf of the firm that is stored in paper copy or electronically for the member’s or candidate’s convenience while employed, however, should be erased or returned to the employer unless the firm gives…

questions.q: A firm announces that its new CEO, "as a CFA charterholder, has superior qualities to manage clients' investments." Under VII(B) this is:
options: Acceptable if the CEO passed all levels on the first attempt
Acceptable, since the charter shows competence
An improper reference: it exaggerates what the designation means
questions.why: Claims of superior performance or ability because of the designation are exaggerations. Referring to the rigor of the program or the skills it cultivates is acceptable.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Under Standard VI(B), a firm's personal trading policies should be:
options: Approved by clients before employees may trade
Disclosed to investors when they ask for them
Kept confidential to protect employees' privacy
questions.why: Members should fully disclose the firm's personal-investing policies to investors on request. Recommended procedures also include IPO restrictions and blackout periods.

questions.q: A fraud stays hidden despite a thorough audit and a clean regulatory inspection. The diligent auditor has most likely:
options: Violated V(A), Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Violated IV(C), Responsibilities of Supervisors
Not violated the Standards
questions.why: The Standards require reasonable efforts, not perfect detection. Missing a well-concealed fraud after diligent work isn't a violation.

questions.q: A full-time analyst also works 30 hours a week as a waitress. The most likely issue is:
options: IV(A) Loyalty: the workload could lower the quality of her work for the employer, although the second job itself is not a violation
None: non-competing outside work never raises an issue
IV(B) Additional Compensation: she must disclose the job to clients
questions.why: A non-competing job is not prohibited, but a heavy workload can deprive the employer of her best work (IV(A)).

vignettes.body:
Better Investments, founded by Ardy Sobhani, CFA, five years ago, is an investment adviser serving mostly middle-income clients along with several high-net-worth clients. Sobhani initially worked alone, but because of rapid growth, Better Investments has expanded to 20 employees today. Better Investments continues to add new clients and recently hired a junior analyst, Shigeru Miyagawa.

Miyagawa is registered for Level I of the CFA exams. He recently learned that Sobhani has been an instructor with a CFA exam prep program for many years, so he asks Sobhani if he can provide any tips on the exam. Sobhani responds, “Our prep course providers looked at the curriculum readings and based on this analysis we do not think you should worry about exotic over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives being tested. Instead focus on the core body of knowledge. CFA Institute has a heavier weighting on equities and fixed-income analysis, and I am sure the exam will always have a similar emphasis.” Miyagawa replies, “when I took the practice exam it seemed to have more weight on alternative investments.”

In a meeting with Spencer Purce, a prospective client who recently sold his business for over $100 million, Sobhani learns that Purce plans to quit working. Purce asks for ideas on how to invest his sale proceeds to build wealth within a trust structure so that he can pass capital on to his twin sons, who are 19-year-old students. Sobhani tells Purce:

Considering your objectives specifically, I looked at infrastructure projects in developing countries for clients interested in diversifying their portfolios with long-duration projects, consistent cash flow, high operating margins, and a positive correlation to inflation. These types of investments require large up-front cash injections, patience, and the ability to accept a long cash out period. But, there are several benefits to this type of investment that I think are important for you, including diversification, exposure to rapidly growing economies, and returns, which are currently in the 8%–12% range, based on my review of similar investments.

Sobhani advises two clients to diversify their portfolios into real estate. He refers them to a licensed attorney who specializes in real estate investments. Sobhani is paid a referral fee by the attorney, which he fully discloses once a client makes an investment. The attorney offered both clients the opportunity to invest in a loan secured by mortgages on three commercial warehouses. One of the clients buys into the lucrative deal, but Sobhani recommends the other client defer his investment because of liquidity constraints. When the liquidity issues are finally resolved, the investment is no longer available.

Reviewing the firm’s bank account, Sobhani notices several unauthorized credit card payments for thousands of dollars. Janis Wilder, Sobhani’s personal assistant, confesses to obtaining a credit card in Sobhani’s name and using this card to fund her personal travels. Local law requires investment advisors to inform their regulators of any employee theft. But, because Wilder is Sobhani’s cousin, he verbally reprimands her: “From now on I will hold the checkbook, and if you ever do something like this again I will report you to the regulators.”

questions.q: When discussing the CFA examination, did either Sobhani or Miyagawa violate the Standard relating to conduct as participants in CFA Institute Programs?
options: Yes, Sobhani violated the Standard
Yes, both Sobhani and Miyagawa violated the Standard
No
questions.why: Correct because the information disclosed about the exams by either Sobhani or Miyagawa is not confidential CFA Program information, so they are not in violation of Standard VII(A), Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs. Sobhani’s information was based upon his analysis of the readings and is his opinion, and Miyagawa referenced the practice exam, which does not reflect content in the actual CFA exam.

questions.q: Sobhani’s advice to Purce with regards to a potential investment is mostconsistent with the Standards concerning which of the following?
options: Suitability
Diligence and Reasonable Basis
Performance Presentation
questions.why: Correct because Sobhani has only stated historical returns for these types of investments based on research of other similar investments. In addition, he has not promised a specific return, so he is not in violation of Standard III(D), Performance Presentation.

questions.q: Concerning his advice related to real estate investments, did Sobhani most likely violate the Standards?
options: Yes, with regard to Referral Fees.
Yes, with regard to Fair Dealing.
No.
questions.why: Correct because Standard VI(C), Referral Fees, requires members and candidates to disclose to their employer, clients, and prospective clients, as appropriate, any compensation, consideration, or benefit received from or paid to others for the recommendation of products or services before entry into any formal agreement for services.

questions.q: With regard to his actions related to Wilder, Sobhani least likely violated the Standard relating to:
options: misconduct.
disclosure of conflicts.
knowledge of the law
questions.why: Correct because Sobhani has not violated Standard VI(A), Disclosure of Conflicts, because disclosure of his relationship with Wilder is not required because it would not impair Sobhani’s independence and objectivity nor interfere with his respective duties to clients.

vignettes.body:
Jacob Kostecka, CFA, is a portfolio manager at Forkson Investment Management, an asset management and research focused organization. After obtaining his CFA charter last month, Kostecka was transferred to the private wealth management division at Forkson.

Dharshi Bope, a private wealth client, was involved in a major motorcycle accident and is in critical condition, fighting for his life. Bope is a single parent with a daughter, Paveen Nathoo, in her mid-twenties. Since the accident, Nathoo has managed her father’s affairs, paying all expenses, including investment advisory fees. In several conversations with Nathoo, Kostecka highlighted Bope’s low risk tolerance and investment goal of capital preservation. Nathoo has indicated her interest in managing the account more aggressively and possibly moving to another management firm. Nathoo recently petitioned the court to appoint her full power of attorney to legally manage Bope’s affairs. Prior to the court decision, Nathoo asks Kostecka to invest her father’s account in the initial public offering (IPO) of Chatterbox, a highly sought after social media company that has yet to generate a profit.

The following week, the court approves Nathoo’s request to act on behalf of her father.

Nathoo establishes a non-discretionary investment account at Forkson tied to her newly established business. Shortly thereafter, Kostecka joins the board of Jabbertalk.com, a smaller social media competitor to Chatterbox. Based on his knowledge of Chatterbox, Kostecka believes the stock of Jabbertalk is a good investment, even though it is not yet profitable. Buoyed by his faith in social media, Kostecka ultimately purchases shares of Jabbertalk’s IPO for Nathoo’s account, as well as for all clients he currently manages. When Kostecka informs Nathoo of the purchase, she expresses concern about her legal responsibilities and lack of accounting knowledge in overseeing the account. Kostecka provides Nathoo a list of recommended professionals he has worked with in the past, including attorneys and accountants. When he was in college 10 years earlier, Kostecka was engaged to one of the attorneys but broke off the relationship prior to their wedding, and one of the accountants was Kostecka’s college roommate. Since then, Kostecka has not had any contact with the lawyer and accountant.

The Jabbertalk investment is profitable on the first day of trading, doubling from its opening price. Kostecka tells his clients the multifactor valuation model used by Forkson shows Jabbertalk stock is still undervalued. Forkson’s research report, due out the next day, will recommend investors hold their Jabbertalk shares. However, Kostecka tells all his clients simultaneously they should sell their shares because he believes Jabbertalk is overvalued and the stock price will fall soon. Kostecka notes he has followed through on this belief by selling his personal holdings of Jabbertalk shares. Nathoo ignores Kostecka’s recommendation to sell Jabbertalk. Over the next week, the stock declines 75%.

Watching Jabbertalk’s severe share price decline, Nathoo becomes furious with Kostecka because he did not sell shares of Jabbertalk in her account. She files a complaint with Kostecka’s supervisor, Sally Fang, CFA, claiming she was misled on the value of the IPO in the days immediately after the stock started trading. Kostecka responds to the complaint by telling Fang, “the analyst who wrote the hold recommendation on Jabbertalk has only passed his CFA Level II examination. As a charterholder, I have earned the right to use the CFA designation, so I am more qualified to manage clients’ investments.”

questions.q: With regard to the investment request made by Nathoo to invest in Chatterbox, Kostecka should most likely:
options: follow Bope’s investment goals.
comply with her request.
seek advice from the court.
questions.why: The account should be managed according to the client’s investment goal of capital preservation and a low risk tolerance. Under Standard III(A) –Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, the first step for members and candidates in fulfilling their duty of loyalty to clients is to determine the identity of the “client” to whom the duty of loyalty is owed.

questions.q: With regard to investing in Jabbertalk and recommending experts, Kostecka most likely needs to disclose conflicts related to his:
options: attorney relationship.
board membership.
accountant relationship.
questions.why: Kostecka’s board service creates the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information involving Jabbertalk and is a basic conflict of interest. As a result, according to Standard VI(A)–Conflicts of Interest, the directorship should be disclosed.

questions.q: In relation to Kostecka’s handling of the Jabbertalk stock recommendation, which of the following CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct did he least likely violate?
options: Priority of Transactions
Communication with Clients
Fair Dealing
questions.why: Standard III(B)–Fair Dealing requires members and candidates to deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities.

questions.q: When Kostecka defends himself against Nathoo’s complaint, he most likely violated the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct concerning the:
options: reference to candidacy in the CFA Program.
misrepresentation of the meaning of the designation.
right to use the CFA designation.
questions.why: Statements overstating the competency of an individual or imply, either directly or indirectly, that superior performance can be expected from someone with the CFA designation are not allowed under Standard VII(B)–Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: Jamison is a junior research analyst with Howard & Howard, a brokerage and investment banking firm. Howard & Howard’s mergers and acquisitions department has represented the Britland Company in all of its acquisitions for the past 20 years. Two of Howard & Howard’s senior officers are directors of various Britland subsidiaries. Jamison has been asked to write a research report on Britland. What is the best course of action for her to follow?
options: Jamison should not write the report because the two Howard & Howard officers serve as directors for subsidiaries of Britland.
Jamison may write the report but must refrain from expressing any opinions because of the special relationships between the two companies.
Jamison may write the report if she discloses the director relationship between the two companies.
questions.why: This question involves Standard VI(A) Avoid or Disclose Conflicts. The question establishes a conflict of interest in which an analyst, Jamison, is asked to write a research report on a company that is a client of her employer. In addition, two directors of the company are senior officers of Jamison’s employer.

questions.q: An asset that is risky on its own is recommended to a risk-averse client. Under III(C) Suitability, this can be acceptable if:
options: The asset is judged on its own, and its risk is within the client's tolerance
The client's total portfolio is ignored
It is judged in the context of the client's total portfolio, and total portfolio risk stays low
questions.why: Suitability is assessed against the whole portfolio. A risky position can be fine if the overall portfolio risk is low.

questions.q: Under IV(B), written consent for an outside paid arrangement must come from:
options: The member's clients and prospects
All parties involved, incl. the employer
The member's former employer only
questions.why: IV(B) Additional Compensation Arrangements requires written consent from all parties involved, which always includes the member's current employer.

questions.q: After leaving a firm with no noncompete, simply knowing the names of its clients is:
options: Generally not confidential information
Confidential, so using them breaches III(E)
Usable only after a cooling-off period
questions.why: Knowing that former clients exist is generally not confidential under IV(A) or III(E), unless a confidentiality agreement or the law says otherwise.

vignettes.body:
Ethics: Standards of Professional Conduct
Independent questions. Each question below stands on its own and does not depend on the others.

questions.q: During a round of golf, Rodriguez, chief financial officer of Mega Retail, mentions to Hart, a local investment adviser and long-time personal friend, that Mega is having an exceptional sales quarter. Rodriguez expects the results to be almost 10% above the current estimates. The next day, Hart initiates the purchase of a large stake in the local exchange-traded retail fund for her personal account.
options: Hart violated the Code and Standards by investing in the exchange-traded fund that included Mega Retail.
Rodriguez did not violate the Code and Standards, because the comments made to Hart were not intended to solicit an investment in Mega Retail.
